records.title: The Iliad
records.author: Homer
records.quote: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans.
records.source: Homer, Iliad I.1, tr. Samuel Butler (1898) — public domain
records.essence: The founding war epic of the West: one man's rage in the tenth year of the Trojan War, and the mortality and honor that drive mortals and gods alike.
records.original: Homeric Greek (~8th c. BCE) — public-domain text via the Perseus Digital Library.
records.translationNote: Every age re-translates Homer — Pope (1715) made him rhyme, Butler (1898) made him prose; the first word, mēnis ('rage'), is famously hard to land.

connections.note: Virgil wrote Rome's epic as a deliberate answer to Homer — Aeneas is the anti-Achilles, duty chosen over rage.
East and West both open on a battlefield: Achilles' wrath and Arjuna's refusal both ask how a warrior should face duty and death.
Homeric glory (kleos), won by force, against Confucian virtue (ren), won by character — two rival ideals of a life worth remembering.

records.title: The Republic
records.author: Plato
records.quote: Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy… cities will never have rest from their evils.
records.source: Plato, Republic V (473d), tr. Benjamin Jowett (1871) — public domain
records.essence: Plato builds an ideal city to discover what justice really is — and argues that only those who love wisdom are fit to hold power.
records.original: Classical Greek (~375 BCE) — public-domain text via the Perseus Digital Library.
records.translationNote: Jowett's Victorian English is the classic version; later translators tighten his long sentences, but the Cave is the Cave in all of them.

connections.note: The same question an ocean apart: Plato's philosopher-king and Confucius's sage-ruler both hold that a state is only as good as the wisdom of whoever governs it.
Plato engineers the perfect city by reason; Laozi says the best ruler governs least (wu-wei) — opposite cures for the same disease.
Augustine turns Plato's eternal Forms toward a Christian God — Platonism baptized.
Marcus's Stoicism descends from the Socratic conviction that the examined life is the only one worth living.

records.title: The Analects
records.author: Confucius
records.quote: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
records.source: Confucius, Analects XV.23, tr. James Legge (1893) — public domain
records.essence: The recorded conversations of Confucius and his students on becoming fully human — through learning, ritual, and ren, human-heartedness.
records.original: Classical Chinese (~5th c. BCE) — public-domain text via the Chinese Text Project.
records.translationNote: Legge (1893) is literal and learned; Waley (1938) made it readable — and 'ren' has been rendered everything from 'benevolence' to 'human-heartedness.'

connections.note: Aristotle and Confucius reach the same place by different roads: virtue is a habit, formed by practice, poised between extremes.
What makes someone fit to rule? Confucius's answer — the cultivated sage — rhymes with Plato's philosopher-king.
Both anchor the good life in duty to one's station — the Confucian roles and the Gita's dharma.

records.title: Confessions
records.author: Saint Augustine
records.quote: Thou hast made us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
records.source: Augustine, Confessions I.1, tr. E. B. Pusey (1838) — public domain
records.essence: The first true autobiography of a soul — a restless, brilliant life turning, at last, toward God.
records.original: Latin (397–400 CE) — public-domain text.
records.translationNote: Pusey (1838) keeps the 'Thou'; modern versions drop it — but 'our heart is restless until it rests in Thee' survives every rendering.

connections.note: Augustine inherits Plato's eternal truths and re-grounds them in a personal God — the Forms become the divine.
Two traditions on the soul's longing for the divine: Augustine's restless heart and the Gita's path of devotion (bhakti).
Augustine finds peace by seeking until he rests in God; Laozi finds it by ceasing to seek — two routes to stillness.

records.title: The Bhagavad Gita
records.quote: Your business is with action alone, not by any means with its fruits.
records.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.47, tr. Kashinath Trimbak Telang (1882, Sacred Books of the East) — public domain
records.essence: On the edge of battle a warrior refuses to fight; the god Krishna answers him — act from duty, without grasping at the outcome.
records.original: Sanskrit (~200 BCE–200 CE), within the Mahabharata — public-domain text.
records.translationNote: Arnold (1885) set it in Victorian verse, 'The Song Celestial'; Telang (1882) kept it literal — verse 2.47 on detached action is the line everyone returns to.

connections.note: Both open on a battlefield where a warrior must decide how to meet duty and death — Arjuna's doubt mirrors Achilles' wrath.
Do what is right and let go of the result — the Gita's karma-yoga and Marcus's Stoicism land on nearly the same discipline, worlds apart.
The soul's longing for the eternal — devotion in the Gita, restlessness-toward-God in Augustine.

records.title: The Aeneid
records.author: Virgil
records.quote: Arms, and the man I sing, who, forced by fate, and haughty Juno's unrelenting hate, expelled and exiled, left the Trojan shore.
records.source: Virgil, Aeneid I.1, tr. John Dryden (1697) — public domain
records.essence: Rome's national epic: a refugee from fallen Troy carries his gods and his son toward Italy to found the race that will become Rome — duty over passion.
records.original: Latin (~29–19 BCE) — public-domain text via the Perseus Digital Library.
records.translationNote: Dryden (1697) made Virgil rhyme in heroic couplets; modern versions free the line — but every one opens on 'arma virumque cano,' 'arms and the man I sing.'

connections.note: Virgil rewrites Homer on purpose — the first half echoes the Odyssey's wandering, the second the Iliad's war, with Roman duty in place of Greek rage.
Aeneas leaving Dido for his destiny and Arjuna doing his duty are the same hard lesson: the call of fate over the heart's desire.
Augustine wept over Dido as a boy (he says so in the Confessions) before he learned to weep for his own soul.

records.title: Meditations
records.author: Marcus Aurelius
records.quote: Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.
records.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 5.16, tr. George Long (1862) — public domain
records.essence: A Roman emperor's private notebook — Stoic reminders to himself on duty, mortality, and the mastery of one's own mind.
records.original: Koine Greek (~170–180 CE) — Lectio carries the Greek original.
records.translationNote: Marcus, a Roman, wrote to himself in Greek; Casaubon (1634) made him ornate, Long (1862) made him plain — the Stoic bones are unchanged.

connections.note: Act rightly and release the outcome — the Gita's karma-yoga and Marcus's Stoicism arrive at nearly the same discipline, worlds apart.
Stoicism grows from the Socratic root Plato planted: the examined life, the soul ordered by reason.
Daily self-correction and the cultivation of character — Marcus's morning reminders echo Confucian self-examination.
Two interior books: Marcus steadies the self by reason, Augustine surrenders it to God.

records.title: The Tao Te Ching
records.author: Laozi
records.quote: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
records.source: Laozi, Tao Te Ching 1, tr. James Legge (1891) — public domain
records.essence: Eighty-one terse verses on the Way that cannot be named, and the power (te) that works by yielding rather than forcing.
records.original: Classical Chinese (~4th c. BCE) — public-domain text via the Chinese Text Project.
records.translationNote: The most-translated Chinese book; the opening line — that the Tao you can name isn't the real Tao — is itself a warning about translation.

connections.note: Plato governs by reason and design; Laozi by wu-wei, ruling least — opposite political visions, East and West.
Within China itself: Confucian striving, ritual, and order against Taoist yielding and naturalness — the two poles of Chinese thought.
Accept the flow of nature rather than fight it — Stoic and Taoist acceptance reaching for the same calm.
Two paths to peace: Augustine by restless seeking until he rests in God, Laozi by ceasing to seek at all.

records.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
records.author: Anonymous · Sumer & Akkad
records.quote: The life you seek you will never find; for when the gods created man, they allotted to him death, but life they kept in their own keeping.
records.source: The Epic of Gilgamesh, Old Babylonian version (Siduri's counsel to Gilgamesh) — public-domain translation
records.essence: The oldest surviving epic: a king's friendship and grief, and his failed quest for immortality — he comes home mortal, and wiser.
records.original: Akkadian, in cuneiform (~2100–1200 BCE) — reconstructed from many broken clay tablets; public-domain editions of the cuneiform exist.
records.translationNote: There is no single 'Gilgamesh' — it survives on broken tablets in several versions, so every translation is also an act of reconstruction.

connections.note: The oldest war-and-grief epic, a root beneath Homer: Enkidu's death prefigures Patroclus', and Gilgamesh's wild grief, Achilles'.
The restless search for what this life cannot give — immortality for Gilgamesh, God for Augustine.
Both face mortality head-on and ask what, if anything, survives it.

records.title: Nicomachean Ethics
records.author: Aristotle
records.quote: Happiness is a certain working of the soul in the way of perfect excellence.
records.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7 (1098a), tr. D. P. Chase (1847) — public domain
records.essence: Aristotle's inquiry into the good life: happiness (eudaimonia) as the soul's activity in excellence, and virtue as a trained habit poised between extremes.
records.original: Classical Greek (~340 BCE) — public-domain text via the Perseus Digital Library.
records.translationNote: The famous line 'we are what we repeatedly do; excellence is a habit' is actually Will Durant summarizing Aristotle — not Aristotle himself. A caution about famous quotes.

connections.note: Virtue as a habit, balanced between extremes — Aristotle and Confucius converge on the same ethics from opposite ends of the world.
Aristotle, Plato's own student, grounds the good in human flourishing here on earth rather than in the eternal Forms.
The Stoic practice of virtue descends from this Greek tradition of character and the well-lived life.
Aristotle seeks happiness through virtuous activity; the Gita seeks release through detached action — two visions of the good life.

records.title: The Odyssey
records.author: Homer
records.quote: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy.
records.source: Homer, Odyssey I.1, tr. Samuel Butler (1900) — public domain
records.essence: The long way home: ten years of wandering, monsters, and cunning as Odysseus fights to return to Ithaca — the West's first great homecoming.
records.original: Homeric Greek (~8th c. BCE) — public-domain text via the Perseus Digital Library.
records.translationNote: Butler (1900) put the Odyssey in plain prose, arguing Homer should read like a story; verse translators from Pope onward disagree — the homecoming survives both.

connections.note: Homer's two halves: the Iliad is war and rage, the Odyssey the long road home — together they frame the whole heroic life.
Virgil's first six books are a deliberate Odyssey — wandering toward a promised land — before the Iliad of war.
Both are journey epics: a hero ranges to the ends of the earth and comes home changed.

records.title: The Divine Comedy
records.author: Dante Alighieri
records.quote: All hope abandon, ye who enter in!
records.source: Dante, Inferno III.9, tr. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1867) — public domain
records.essence: A journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise — the summit of the medieval imagination, guided first by Virgil, then by love itself.
records.original: Medieval Tuscan Italian (~1308–1320) — public-domain text.
records.translationNote: Dante wrote in Italian, not Latin, to reach ordinary readers — the original 'vernacular.' Longfellow (1867) and Cary (1814) are the great public-domain English versions.

connections.note: Dante takes Virgil himself as his guide through Hell — the Aeneid's underworld (Book VI) is the model for the whole descent.
Both chart a soul's road from sin to God — Augustine in memory, Dante in vision.
Each stages the soul's journey to the divine as a guided dialogue — Dante led by Virgil and Beatrice, Arjuna by Krishna.

records.title: The Prince
records.author: Niccolò Machiavelli
records.quote: It is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with.
records.source: Machiavelli, The Prince XVII, tr. W. K. Marriott (1908) — public domain
records.essence: A cold, clear handbook on how power is actually won and kept — politics described as it is, not as it ought to be.
records.original: Italian (1513) — public-domain text.
records.translationNote: Marriott's 1908 English is the standard public-domain version — and the 'feared than loved' line is almost always quoted shorn of his careful 'if you must choose between the two.'

connections.note: Plato asks how a state *ought* to be ruled by the wise and good; Machiavelli, how it *is* ruled by those who keep power — the great split in political thought.
Two unsentimental manuals of power — Sun Tzu on the battlefield, Machiavelli in the court.
Confucius says a ruler holds power by virtue and the people's trust; Machiavelli, by fear and necessity — East and West on what a ruler owes.

records.title: The Dhammapada
records.author: Early Buddhist tradition
records.quote: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
records.source: Dhammapada I.1, tr. F. Max Müller (1881, Sacred Books of the East) — public domain
records.essence: The Buddha's path at its plainest — the mind makes the world, craving makes the suffering, and a way out exists.
records.original: Pali (~3rd c. BCE) — public-domain text.
records.translationNote: Müller (1881) brought the Pali Dhammapada into English for his Sacred Books of the East; later versions still split over 'dhamma' itself — law, truth, teaching, way.

connections.note: Two Indian paths: the Gita acts within the world through detached duty; the Dhammapada steps off the wheel of craving altogether.
Both teach release rather than striving — let go, and suffering loosens its grip.
Master your own judgments and you master your world — the Buddha and the Stoic agree on where the work happens.

records.title: The Art of War
records.author: Sun Tzu
records.quote: Supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting.
records.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War III, tr. Lionel Giles (1910) — public domain
records.essence: Thirteen terse chapters: the best victory is won before the battle — by knowledge, position, and deception rather than force.
records.original: Classical Chinese (~5th c. BCE) — public-domain text via the Chinese Text Project.
records.translationNote: Giles (1910) is the scholarly public-domain standard; the wildly popular 'subdue the enemy without fighting' line is a looser paraphrase of his careful wording.

connections.note: Two manuals of hard-eyed power a world and millennia apart — Sun Tzu on war, Machiavelli on rule.
Homer glorifies the clash of heroes; Sun Tzu would call that a failure — the masterstroke is to win before a sword is drawn.
Winning by yielding, acting without forcing — Sun Tzu's strategy is Taoist wu-wei applied to war.

records.title: Don Quixote
records.author: Miguel de Cervantes
records.quote: In a village of La Mancha, the name of which I have no desire to call to mind, there lived not long since one of those gentlemen that keep a lance in the lance-rack.
records.source: Cervantes, Don Quixote I.1, tr. John Ormsby (1885) — public domain
records.essence: The first modern novel: an aging gentleman, his head full of chivalric romances, rides out to revive knighthood — and the world refuses to play along.
records.original: Spanish (1605–1615) — public-domain text.
records.translationNote: Ormsby (1885) is the great Victorian public-domain Quixote; beware the famous 'dream the impossible dream / see life as it should be' lines — those are from the musical Man of La Mancha, not Cervantes.

connections.note: Dante journeys through a real cosmos of fixed meaning; Quixote rides a disenchanted world where the meaning is only in his head — medieval certainty giving way to modern doubt.
Homer's heroes really are heroes; Quixote only thinks he is — the mock-epic is the heroic epic turned inside out.
Both weigh the gap between the ideal and the actual self — Confucian cultivation toward the gentleman, Quixote's doomed attempt to *become* his ideal.

records.title: Hamlet
records.author: William Shakespeare
records.quote: To be, or not to be: that is the question.
records.source: Shakespeare, Hamlet III.1 (c. 1600) — public domain (original English)
records.essence: A prince, a murdered father, a command for revenge — and a mind so alive to every consequence that it cannot act. Shakespeare's deepest study of thought and paralysis.
records.original: Early Modern English (~1600) — the original; no translation needed for English readers.
records.translationNote: Hamlet needs no English translation — but it has been carried into nearly every language; Schlegel's German Hamlet became almost a national poem of its own.

connections.note: Two Renaissance minds undone from within — Faustus by forbidden knowledge, Hamlet by too much of the ordinary kind.
Both circle death and the worth of action — but Marcus steadies himself to act, while Hamlet thinks himself out of it.
Two princes frozen before a fateful act: Arjuna is moved to do his duty, Hamlet paralyzed by his — East and West on thought and action.

records.title: The Wealth of Nations
records.author: Adam Smith
records.quote: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
records.source: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations I.2 (1776) — public domain
records.essence: The founding work of modern economics: how the division of labor and self-interest, guided as if by an invisible hand, create the wealth of a nation.
records.original: English (1776) — the original.
records.translationNote: Written in plain 18th-century English; the phrase everyone knows — the 'invisible hand' — appears just once in the whole book, almost in passing.

connections.note: Marx wrote Capital as the great counter-argument: Smith's invisible hand, he said, hides exploitation rather than harmony.
Plato orders the economy from above by the wisdom of rulers; Smith says order emerges from below, from millions of self-interested choices.
Both describe people as they actually are — driven by interest — rather than as moralists wish them to be.

records.title: Genesis
records.author: The Bible
records.quote: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
records.source: Genesis 1:1, King James Version (1611) — public domain
records.essence: The Bible's first book: creation, the fall, the flood, and the founding families of Israel — the headwaters of the Western religious imagination.
records.original: Biblical Hebrew (~1200–500 BCE) — public-domain Masoretic text.
records.translationNote: The King James (1611) shaped English itself — 'let there be light' and dozens of everyday phrases come from it; the earlier Tyndale version it drew on cost the translator his life.

connections.note: The flood is older than the Bible: Noah's ark closely echoes the Mesopotamian deluge in Gilgamesh — the same flood, two faiths.
Augustine spends the last books of the Confessions meditating, line by line, on the opening of Genesis.
Two visions of beginnings: Genesis opens with creation out of nothing by one God; Indian thought turns instead on cycles with no first moment.

records.title: The Rubaiyat
records.author: Omar Khayyam
records.quote: The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, moves on: nor all thy Piety nor Wit shall lure it back to cancel half a Line.
records.source: Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, tr. Edward FitzGerald (1859) — public domain
records.essence: A Persian astronomer-poet's quatrains on wine, doubt, and the fleeting day — made world-famous by a Victorian Englishman's loose, luminous rendering.
records.original: Persian (quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam, ~11th–12th c.) — public-domain text.
records.translationNote: FitzGerald (1859) is less a translation than a re-creation — he fused Khayyam's separate quatrains into one poem; scholars still argue how much is Khayyam and how much is FitzGerald.

connections.note: Across four thousand years, the same counsel: life is short and death certain, so taste the day — Siduri's advice to Gilgamesh, sung again in Persian.
Both keep the brevity of life steadily in view — Marcus to steel himself to duty, Khayyam to savor the passing hour.
Each makes peace with impermanence rather than fighting it — the fleeting moment accepted, even embraced.
